text: Medical Mirror

Dongui Bogam (Treasured Mirror of Eastern Medicine), Herbal Medicine Section, Volume One

[Stamp: Chosŏn Government-General Hospital Library]

Composed by Royal Physician of Loyal, Diligent, Upright, and Bright merit, Holder of the Senior First Rank, Duke of Yangpyeong, Heo Jun, by Royal Command

Introductory Examples for Decoctions

Methods of Gathering Medicines

[The text discusses methods of drying medicinal herbs:]

"Shade-drying" means to dry without exposing to direct sunlight — as when water [moisture] is involved, [the herbs] must not be rushed.

"Sun-drying" (暴乾) means to place [the herbs] in direct sunlight to dry in the sun.

As for gathering medicines: In the 2nd and 8th months — that is, spring and autumn — stems, leaves, dry [material], and adhesive [substances] should be collected and processed. [Herbs gathered] in the 2nd month and dried in the shade should be dried over fire if needed; [those gathered] in the 10th month are best. As for all medicines gathered before the 8th month, they may then be collected. Those gathered after that date that are sun-dried are easily obtained, though of inferior quality, until the good months come.

Roots of trees and grasses, even if shade-dried throughout, should be pressed when dry. Material already deteriorated that is gathered should be dried over fire; such material is easily obtained but inferior, until the good months.

Three Grades of Medicinal Properties

Upper-grade medicines, 120 kinds, serve as sovereign drugs that nourish life in accordance with Heaven. They are non-toxic, and taking them in large amounts or over a long period does not harm people. These are for those who wish to lighten the body, boost energy, resist aging, and extend life. These are recorded in the Upper Classic.

Middle-grade medicines, 120 kinds, serve as minister drugs that nourish one's nature in accordance with Humanity. They may or may not be toxic, and one must judge their appropriate use carefully. These are for those who wish to suppress illness and supplement weakness. These are recorded in the Middle Classic.

Lower-grade medicines, 125 kinds, serve as assistant and courier drugs that treat disease in accordance with Earth. Most are toxic and should not be taken for long periods. These are for those who wish to eliminate cold, heat, and pathogenic qi, break up accumulations, and cure illness. These are recorded in the Lower Classic.

The three grades together total 365 kinds, corresponding to 365 degrees, one degree for each day, forming one year. Doubled, the total comes to 730 names.

Six Aged Excellent Medicines

Evodia fruit (吳茱萸), Wolfsbane (狼毒), Unripe bitter orange (枳實), Aged tangerine peel (陳橘皮), Pinellia (半夏), Ephedra (麻黃)

These six medicines are best when aged and old, because their nature is fierce and may harm people when fresh. When fresh, their qi is concentrated and intense; only after aging do they become mild and gentle in their potency.

Methods of Processing and Preparation

In all processing and preparation of medicines, the key lies in understanding the disease; the governing of treatment lies in the power of the medicine. For certain flowing conditions, the concern is not merely the disease; wine-based treatment depends on the hand's technique as well.

Evodia (吳茱萸) is commonly used in households; for treatment, it is appropriate to stir-fry Pinellia until the outer skin is fully processed and its potency is moderated. For diseases located below the throat and above the diaphragm:

Pine bark must be washed with wine to neutralize its toxicity. For serious illness, one must stir-fry. For rhubarb (大黃), one must know that it is a medicine for descending stomach qi. For prolonged weakness, it is charred to powder.

Seeds must be blast-roasted to neutralize toxicity. Fresh ones must be soaked in wine and sun-dried, lest cold damage the stomach qi. As for prepared rehmannia (熟地黃), used over a long period —

They must be combined and used together, soaked in wine and sun-dried.

This passage is from a Chinese herbal medicine text (Dongui Bogam, Liquid Medicines section) describing methods of processing and preparing medicinal herbs. The content covers:

Huojiu (grain alcohol) is used for soaking and steeping; decoctions are similarly prepared by boiling. Stir-frying and processing with Danggui (Angelica sinensis) removes toxicity and promotes dispersal. Nine times steaming and nine times sun-drying is a method of processing; roasting with clarified butter (su) is another preparation method for use.

For liver channel medicines: soaking in vinegar is a processing method. Entering the intestines requires specific preparation. Xiangfu (cyperus) is prepared and placed accordingly; the preparation method must be used with童便 (boys' urine) and salt for administration.

For reducing stagnation: using water with ginger, boiling with童便 (boys' urine), drying, processing with vinegar, soaking overnight for deficiency conditions is appropriate.

Regarding Danggui (Angelica): it guides to the blood, addresses fatigue and channel stagnation; used with salt water, boiled in wine or vinegar for administration.

For Banxia (Pinellia): processing removes toxicity; used to treat phlegm conditions. Soaking in ginger juice makes it transparent. It supplements the kidney, regulates qi, and promotes flow.

Regarding Renzhu, Fuling, Maren, Lianzi, Wuyao, Zhishi and similar herbs: improper preparation causes restlessness and agitation. Taoren (peach kernel) processed correctly resolves fullness.

Regarding double kernels and removing skin and tips from seeds to prevent rashes: soaking ginger, processing Banxia, Fuling, Chenpi, Taoren is done to regulate qi.

Regarding Shen (ginseng): if unable to move through, use Shanzha to resolve toxicity; Huacao fruit with vinegar eliminates this.

Coptis (Huanglian): According to the skin and herb [entries], it counteracts [certain substances], reduces pus and blood [accumulation], tonifies [the body]. With black morning glory (Heichou): it benefits the stomach and black [conditions]. With gardenia (Zhizi): it stops bleeding. With Sichuan Coptis (Chuanlian): it aids the seedling [of the herb] and treats distant [conditions]. With Yuanzhi (Polygala): it is non-toxic and reaches wind [conditions]. With dried Acorus (Chenpu): [used together].

Processing methods: Stir-fry or use in decoction to make it penetrate (e.g., with Mirabilite/saltpeter, stir-fry with brine, steam with bamboo juice, steam with ginseng antler and Huoxiang, stir-fry into Ten-Thousand Decoction, add to the decoction's medicinal steaming).

For removing toxins and treating sores from fire: use Evodia (Wuzhuyu) as the chief [herb]; use floating specimens for [addressing] upward [rising conditions]; use sinking specimens for [addressing] downward [conditions]; grind into fine powder; soak in milk to make pills; take with cinnabar.

Croton seed (Badou): take the kernel, two qian, remove the shell and oil; form into round pills; with cinnabar, one fen; fine powder applied to the scalp area for darkening and moistening; take the best sun-dried [preparation]; for sinews, moisten [them]; processed with Du [herb] for raw use.

For various medicinal preparations: stir-fry to remove the tendency to move without generating [new qi]; use fine powder for use; process with vinegar and Aconite accessory root (Fuzi) for various medicinal uses; stir-fry with vinegar to make the substance real; use the juice to stir-fry to remove [the tendency] to move without generating [new qi]; use fine powder for application; process with Eucommia (Du) for raw use.

Methods of Preparing Medicines

The fixed method of a formula requires fermented wine; stir-fry with tea and coptis; rinse with water; use raw below; use on the face; use nine [ingredients].

Regarding the skin and flesh, processed medicines descend and moisten, while raw medicines rise and dry.

On the method of sovereign, minister, assistant, and envoy in a formula: What does this mean? Qibo said: The herb that governs the disease is called the sovereign; that which assists the sovereign is called the minister; that which responds to the minister is called the envoy. It is not merely about whether the disease is mild or severe — this applies to the upper, middle, and lower classifications of disease, and to the three grades of medicines.

The sovereign, assistant, and the three daily doses; the feeding schedule; the grade of the preparation; following the ministers in responding — the assistant serves the minister, and the envoy responds to the minister; the method follows the severity of the disease; what is not inferior is considered of high grade.

The emperor asked what is meant by sovereign and assistant; the assistant of the sovereign is the minister; this method addresses disease; upper, middle, and lower — three grades are distinguished.

That which is called the chief praises the sick person — this is the sovereign; that which assists the sovereign is the minister; that which directs the minister is the assistant; the sovereign herb has ministers responding to it, using assistants and envoys. When composing a formula with many ingredients, if one sovereign, three ministers — they must be complementary and valued.

It is appropriate for the envoy to be numerous; when combining, the sovereign is the chief drug; those that support the disease become ministers; the assistant of the sovereign becomes the minister; the envoy of the minister is the assistant; if one makes a formula, the most numerous is the sovereign, and the ministers are many with few assistants.

When ministers are many and assistants few, the strength is insufficient to encompass prevention with medicine; the sovereign is processed, such as processed Coptis — the sovereign should be most numerous; if the formula has many, three sovereigns and few ministers.

With many ministers, in the middle domain, the sovereign of Coptis is used processed, and also for treating wind-damp; the sovereign herb processed — such as prepared Aconite and Poria — the sovereign is most numerous.

As for the ministers and assistants — this is the category. Using five or six processed [ingredients]; combining yin and yang, using the sovereign with three or four parts in ten; outside those parts there are ministers; adding ginger and reducing the count by seven, same as eight.

As for assistant and envoy herbs: there are those used alone (single action), those that are mutually reinforcing (mutual need), those that assist each other (mutual use), those that are mutually antagonistic (mutual aversion), those that counteract each other (mutual opposition), and those that neutralize each other's toxicity (mutual suppression). [Examples include] ginger, transforming [herbs], precious [herbs], and grasses.

Methods for Decoctions, Powders, and Pills

When medicinal ingredients have mutual aversion or mutual antagonism, or when they provoke each other's toxicity, these seven types of interactions (the "seven relations") must be considered when combining and harmonizing them. If any toxic substances are present, all formulas should use appropriate counterparts.

When preparing household formulas, one may divide the portions differently; the weights and measures listed are not to be rigidly treated as fixed — do not say "combine" or "use the drug" without thought. In nine-ingredient formulas, the portions should be balanced according to the role of sovereign, minister, and assistant herbs. When the illness improves, the balance of the two portions must be even.

Regarding the flavor of cinnabar and the use of sweetroot (licorice) and mountain herbs: if they are administered without careful dosing, they cannot bring out the full effect; if vomited up due to coldness or incompleteness, they are difficult to use. Yellow [ginger] also, when used without the proper method, will not pass through properly. Bamboo sap (zhuli) likewise, if not combined with ginger, its nature cannot be fully expressed.

When preparing medicines that are dry-natured, they should tonify the blood and aid the decoction; bamboo sap should not be used without ginger, as it will not move through properly.

For those like hemp seed (huma) and poria (fuling) that are to be decocted, some should be made into powder with ginger, some should be boiled in water, and some cannot be added to a decoction.

Some ingredients, like small red beans (chixiaodou) and hemp seeds, in formulas of three, six, or nine [units], large or small, coarse or fine — these distinctions must be carefully followed.

Regarding preparations the size of large soybeans: mix powder with honey; if it is the size of a firmiana (parasol tree) seed, use two large soybeans as the standard measure.
For a square-inch spoon of powder mixed with honey, two measures equal the size of a pellet; use two large soybeans as the standard.
For elderly patients, the standard formula uses seven-tenths; to achieve the proper measure, use nine [units] equaling two large soybeans as standard.

Regarding decoctions with medicine: adjust the knife-measure to seven parts; the correct formula is to take [the amount] equal to a firmiana seed — nine [units] equal to large soybeans as standard.

For rubbing applications of medicine: the formula states to use tiger [fat] as a base; take a standard amount equal to pine-firmiana seeds — nine [units] equal to large soybeans.

Regarding oral dosing: as stated, use hemp [seed size] as reference — one dose; six parts obtained; take [the amount] — not exceeding the standard; measure in two parts then decoct; raise to one [sheng]; ten yun [units] of powder.

For knife-measure decoctions: use bean-sized amounts; finely bite/crush; below one [unit]; six parts; eight fen; then one sheng of medicine; one sheng, ten yun of powder.

Water intake: use iron vessels; crush to fine powder; swallow with large amounts; bring together into a vessel; this is easily prepared as a powder poultice.

Stop [the medicine] when: the taste is removed, thinned; when disease is treated with congee; store in a repository; accumulate greatly; this is easily prepared — disperse, poultice, hemp; prepare as a decoction; this is the method. Ancient classic formula.

For the qi [vital energy]: large [dose] — exemption applies; rounded pills; combine with dregs; for storage accumulation; apply the qi; coarsely ground, fine, raw — make into a decoction; this is the preparation method.

For steaming [preparations]: use ginger juice; collect finely; prepare steamed cake.

For treating toxicity: use Arisaema (南星, nanxing); make into nine-and-a-half [pills]; take the desired [dose]; remove [impurities]; concentrate; wash; use raw ginger; store overnight; steam; make into a cake with the juice; collect finely.

Seven Formulas

[The text describes the classical Chinese medical theory of the "Seven Formulas" (七方), which categorizes prescriptions into seven types:]

Those [pills] that are taken are easy to transform; refined honey-pills, when taken rotationally, achieve their effect gradually.
Aqueous preparations (decoctions/tang) are given to clear and disperse; pills are for chronic conditions that are difficult to treat — taken gradually, in powder or scattered form, administered rotationally.
Decoctions work by being gradual and moderate; they cannot quickly expel disease; their use is to achieve a slow, thorough effect.
The meaning of this is as follows: large and small refer to the pace — urgent or gradual. Sealed cinnabar preparations are gradual. Pills are again easy to transform and dissolve when refined with honey.

The Seven Formulas: A formula with one ruler (chief herb) and two ministers — this is the large formula. A formula with three ingredients combined into a small formula. A formula with one ruler and two ministers is the supplementing-downward formula.

Regarding the Seven Formulas and nine preparations: large and small refer to urgency and gradualism. A formula with one ruler and two ministers for gradual action; if not large, it is an odd-numbered formula. Gradual without excessive frequency — a formula with one ruler and two ministers is a compound formula; a small formula.

Supplementing downward and upward in regulation — urgent regulation; not gradual, not excessive in frequency; for multiple types of conditions; even-numbered formulas.

Compound formulas: three downward, combining substances together, two forming one formula — just like the Two Sages Powder, five-to-eight types, even-numbered formulas.

A formula with two rulers and one minister is an even pair; three ministers. A formula with one ruler, three ministers, and five assistants is a regulated formula.

Six regulations, not paired — two ministers, four regulations, paired, small, large — one minister to one.

The ruler-formula uses the descending regulation; hence it is called "regulated"; removing the large; one ruler, two, one.

Adjustment uses the strange (odd) and the lower; the strange force, unflavored, gradually supplementing, ascending mildly; treating with distant regulation using even-paired two-regulation formulas.

One ruler, one minister, assistant — nine regulations of the large; distant even-paired ancient odd-numbered compound large formulas; their supplementation reaches this treatment.

The Twelve Formulas

In herbal medicine, there is the method of the Ten Formulas: those that are appropriate (宜), those that unblock (通), those that tonify (補), those that drain (瀉), those that are light (輕), those that are heavy (重), those that are slippery (滑), those that are astringent (澀), those that dry (燥), and those that are dampening (濕). The original classic does not discuss the "appropriate" category explicitly. The later category of percolating dampness also belongs to the tonifying formulas. Belonging to the drying category are things like ginger and atractylodes. Belonging to the heavy category are things like oyster shell and dragon bone, which can eliminate dampness.

In the unblocking formulas, the appropriate medicines are those that unblock. The original classic does not discuss the light category explicitly. The later percolating category is also a subcategory. Belonging here are things like ephedra, which drains. Belonging to the method of elimination are ginger, atractylodes, and stephania. Belonging to the weakening category is the human component.

Ginseng and mutton are medicines; ephedra belongs to the draining category and can eliminate; ginger, atractylodes, and stephania belong to the elimination method; the weakening subcategory belongs to the human element.

Magnetite and light powder can eliminate; winter mallow and elm bark belong here; oyster shell and dragon bone can eliminate dampness.

For the nine messenger herbs, they act quickly; preparations like chicken-head grain are controlled; large-dose heart-warming decoctions should be boiled and taken; excess moisture should be dried out; the ten expelling agents drive out and regulate, combining into a large formula.

For treating with nine herbs: use decoctions and pills; for conditions of yin deficiency and acid regurgitation with cold and flat sensations in the liver and lower regions, use huang (yellow herbs), add bupleurum, decoct in water, with the chief herb known; take by sips; with gentian to control vomiting; for bitter cold conditions, take nine doses; replenish the essence.

Take the superficial symptoms first; stop here; then reduce and gradually ease; take the nine pills; drink the decoction; use acupuncture when urgent; do not be averse to frequent dosing for stubborn conditions.

For the few versus the many: when there are few sovereign and minister herbs, use gradual and mild approaches; treat the heart at its root; for nearby conditions treat locally; for guest-type disorders use decoctions urgently and frequently; do not be averse to frequent doses for stubborn conditions.

For large versus small dosing: when the formula is large, use fewer doses; when small, use two doses; for the minor kidney and liver conditions, use distant administration via decoctions and powders; do not be averse to frequent dosing for stubborn conditions.

Weights and Measures: Jin (斤), Liang (兩), Sheng (升), Dou (斗)

All medicines should be fully processed (熟). It is permissible to use alone. Remove coldness. That is, Aconite (附子), Cinnamon Bark (宮桂) — these belong to the warm/hot category. Cold medicines can remove stagnation; that is, Amethyst (紫石英) and cold-natured herbs belong to this category. In contemporary village practice, these are supplemented accordingly. These two categories belong to warm-heat and cold natures.

Regarding the two types: Mulberry root bark (桑白皮) and Red Adzuki Bean (赤小豆) belong to the warm category. How can cold herbs be left out? Today's practitioners supplement these accordingly. These also belong to the cold-heat distinction.

Concerning ancient weight units: An ancient "ting" (鋌) equals six "cheng" (稱). Only one ting is divided into four liang and four fen. Today, six liang equals ten liang, which equals one "tai" (泰). One ting is derived from one fen of tai. This refers to one-twelfth of a liang.

Regarding the copper-based weight standard: one liang equals sixteen zhu (銖); ten liang equals one tai; one qian (千) equals one.

Today's standard: one liang equals two and a half [smaller units]; two liang equals one-half of two fen; ten liang equals sixteen.

Old and new weight comparisons: One huan (鍰) equals one zhu (銖); two wen (文) equals sixteen; one large unit equals one huan, one zhu, or a counterfeit weight; eight liang equals one huan.

Explanatory notes on accumulated weights: Six, ten, fourteen ting equal one jian (監); four, eight liang equal one qian; ten, fourteen equal large standard weights; eighteen equal yupfen (玉粉); nine yuan; thirty days; half a zhu.

Regarding the dan (丹) and measurements of water, sheng, and jin: One modern jin equals the old large standard jin. According to the medical encyclopedia (醫鑑), these have been in use.

Method of Decocting Medicine

When preparing medicine, first take a measured amount of clean water appropriate to the patient's condition. When decocting medicine for a person, one must choose the proper vessel, control the heat, and bring the medicine to a proper boil, doing so with sincerity and full attention.

If the task is left carelessly to an inattentive person, there will be insufficient patience and the oil will not be removed; slow fire decoction is required. Only clean water and fine silk-strained water should be used.

[Measurements and proportions for various vessel sizes and decoction amounts follow, specifying cups, ounces, and portions.]

For drying decoctions: when using stone vessels, remove the dregs, measure the juice and water. Decoct until reduced. Do not let it become too condensed. Sweating-inducing and purgative medicines should be decocted to a full cup; tonic medicines should be decocted to one and a half cups. The dregs may be re-decocted with water and taken again.

For dry preparations: similarly adjust the amount of water according to whether the medicine is a tonic, a diaphoretic, or a purgative. Decoct until reduced to the appropriate fraction. For tonic medicines requiring much water, take a small amount at a time.

Methods for Taking Medicine

When decocting medicines such as Jia-ji-zhuo (complex decoctions), one should simmer them to reduce the liquid and concentrate the juice. Use a large jujube to treat dispersing conditions. For high-level cold diseases, use scallion whites to dispel dampness. Use five qian of medicine to one measure of water. For dispersing formulas, bring to one or two boils and take in one dose with water.

For those with deficiency, the current standard is to use five qian of medicine with water. According to the old formula, use half that amount, prepare once, and take with water in one or two boilings.

For burn injuries: the primary medicinal should first be decocted; for eye conditions involving sweating, first decoct ephedra until one or two boils have occurred.

For wind-damp injuries, first decoct ginger and saposhnikovia root. For wood-wind conditions that are non-toxic, for summerheat disorders, first decoct cinnamon twig and harmonizing medicines; first decoct bupleurum and scutellaria.

For toxic and non-toxic medicines: use approximately this method of decocting first.

Regarding the timing of medicine intake: if there is damage from toxic substances, treat it by removing the toxin from the flesh and fruit. For nourishing the body after illness, do not take too much; after illness, the mind may become dulled.

The wise physician instructs the patient to eat beforehand; for conditions in the four limbs and blood, use medicine after removing pathology; for abdominal conditions, treat the abdomen first.

Clear medicines should be taken on an empty stomach; for conditions in the lower body, nourish from below.

For bone marrow conditions, take urgently with food; for upper-body conditions, a gradual approach with food is appropriate.

Regarding dosage: for more doses, use tonic medicines for upper-body conditions; for concentrated lower-body decoctions, take in larger amounts. For drastic tonification of the lower body, do not take excessively. Large doses should be taken nine times in a concentrated form.

Five Flavors of Medicines

When taking medicines, if it is a cold medicine, drink it warm; if it is a hot medicine, take it cold — this seeks a balanced, harmonious preparation. Even tonifying kidney medicines can be difficult to swallow if taken improperly.

Regarding yang medicines: they must be taken hot. Regarding yin medicines: they must be taken cold. Initially one speaks of taking them down with cold liquid, but one must not rush too hastily. There are five key principles. If taken improperly, even tonifying kidney medicines will be hard to receive.

On the properties of medicines: Medicines such as cinnamon bark belong to the category of feathers and fur — they soften when combined with scallions and become pliable; the nature of cypress and platycodon, when combined, can be counteracted when combined with lacquer and hemp.

On the colors of medicines: Cinnabar corresponds to fire, so its color is red, belonging to yang, governing the heart. It corresponds to wood, so its color is green, governing the liver. Yellow orpiment corresponds to earth, so its color is yellow, governing the spleen and stomach. White medicines correspond to metal, so their color is white, governing the lungs. Black medicines correspond to water, so their color is black, governing the kidneys.

The five flavors — acrid, sweet, sour, bitter, salty — each have their yin and yang aspects: some are dispersing, some are astringent, some promote movement, some harmonize. When their qi and flavors are combined and taken together, they nourish the five organs.

The five grains nourish; the five fruits assist; the five meats benefit; the five vegetables supplement. When their qi and flavors are combined and taken together, they replenish the essence and boost the qi.

The five flavors — pungent, sour, sweet, bitter, and salty — each have their appropriate seasons and their relationships to the five viscera. They may disperse, astringe, moderate, firm, or soften. The salty flavor, the sour, sweet, bitter, and salty each correspond to the seasons and to diseases of the five viscera; one should use the five flavors appropriately according to the illness, governing the five palaces of the body.

Excess of the sour flavor first enters and damages the liver; its proper function is to enter through the mouth. The five flavors enter the five viscera, with pungent first entering in winter, each returning to govern its palace.

If salty is taken in excess, it first enters and injures the kidneys, accumulating and causing imbalance; this increases the visceral qi and over time creates bias and damage to the organs.

Excess use leads to depletion of the stored essence; the qi becomes weakened over time, imbalanced in the viscera and bowels, and through prolonged use the lung is affected.

When flavors are used in excess, depletion of the stored essence results, leading to sudden damage, wasting, and deterioration — this is how the qi is defeated.

Sourness can astringe and moisten; it softens hardness. Sweetness can moderate and harmonize, facilitate movement downward, and disperse. Bitterness can dry and firm; it can consolidate and help food be digested. Pungency can scatter and disperse; it can move upward and promote circulation. Saltiness can soften hardness and guide things downward.

Bitterness firms and dries. Pungency disperses and moves outward through the surface and interior, stopping accumulation and benefiting the qi upward. Sweetness moves through the channels, nourishing and supplementing, moderating and warming. These are the fundamental natures of the five flavors governing the bones, muscles, and visceral qi, regulating the small intestines, promoting rising and astringing, and nourishing the body throughout.

Rising and Descending of Qi and Flavor

○ When the color is full and dark, this governs Kidney Qi. If the flavor is not balanced and is excessively bitter, the spleen and stomach's intent becomes impaired, yet Stomach Qi remains sovereign.

○ The proper governing flavor is pungent. When not counterbalanced, it opens and disperses the interstices and membranes, allowing the spirit and essence to thrive.

Among the various flavors: if sour is excessive it damages the Liver; if salty is excessive it damages the Heart; if sweet is excessive it damages the Spleen; if bitter is excessive it may benefit the Lungs; pungent flavors enter the Kidneys. These proportions determine health.

Among pungent and bitter tastes: garlic is pungently hot, ginger is hot. All five flavors when excessive harm the corresponding organs.

○ Yang is Qi; Yin is Flavor. Flavor exits through the lower orifices; Qi exits through the upper orifices. The clear and thin is Yin within Yang. The clear and thick is pure Yang. The thin disperses and vents outward; the thick generates heat. The turbid and thin is Yang within Yin; the turbid and thick is pure Yin. The thin opens passages; the thick nourishes and enriches.

○ Clear Yang opens the interstices; Turbid Yin exits through the membranes. Clear Yang fills the four limbs; Turbid Yin returns to the six bowels. Clear Yang rises to the upper orifices; Turbid Yin descends to the lower orifices.

Thin-flavored substances are Yin within Yang. Thick-flavored substances are pure Yin. Thin-Qi substances are Yin within Yang. Thick-Qi substances are pure Yang.

○ Pungent, sweet, and bland flavors belong to Yang. Sour, bitter, and salty flavors belong to Yin.

Yang floats upward; therefore thin-flavored substances belong to Yang. Descending action is also associated with Yang when warmth is stored. Clear thin substances rise and vent outward; thick clear substances are pure Yang. When Qi is thin and Yin, together they form pure Yang. With thick Qi and clear-rising flavor, Yang Qi opens the interstices.

When Yang is dispersed downward, thin-flavored substances belong to Yin within Yang. When Yin floats, thin substances become pure Yin in terms of Qi. Thick flavor enables Yin to flow through, while thin substances flare upward; thus thin Qi vents heat — this is what is meant by thin flavor and perspiration moistening.

Being of a descending nature, Yin is cool. Cold belongs to the Yin of Heaven; warmth and Yang flare upward. Hence thin Qi vents heat. The meaning of perspiration arising from thin Yin is that pure Yin Qi becomes exhausted. Whether flavor is Yin depends on circumstance.

Yang pertains to Yin in its restraining aspect, with little Yin; it therefore flows through and is beneficial. The thin flares up; thin Qi is thus Yin within Yang. Warm, cool, cold, and hot — these are examples. The thick generates heat, and thick-flavored substances that are heat-generating are called such because they are thin-flavored in terms of pure Yin Qi.

This is a passage from classical Chinese medicine theory, dealing with the properties of medicinal substances according to the Yin-Yang and Qi-flavor framework:

Flavor is the image of taste. Sweet and bland, fine and thin, belong to the yang aspect of earth. Sour and bitter belong to the yin of heaven. Salty belongs to the yin of earth. When flavor is thin, it is light and clear. Pungent and bland thin flavors belong to the category of earth, and through the root they connect to sourness. Bitter, salty, and hot belong to the ground. Flavor that is thick and salty, hot, bitter, sweet, cold, or warm — this is flavor in its fullness. Thin flavor belongs to yin within yang; when flavor is thick it promotes discharge. Pungent, sweet, bland, and neutral flavors, when the qi is thin, allow passage through. Sour, bitter, and salty cold flavors represent the thickness of yin. Thin flavors belong to yang within yin. When qi is thin it moves through. Yin within yang — when flavor is thick, the herbs of the Materia Medica do not speak of "bland" as a separate flavor, yet neutral is also present.

Cold, hot, cold — the same region belongs to yang among the five. When qi is thin it promotes bitterness; when flavor is thick it calms and clears, rising subtly. Cold herbs also ascend, clearing and separating. Nourishing through the ying (nutritive qi) to assist the descent, clearing the yang, truly — this is clearing. Yang among the five, thin qi, clearing and calming — clearing within turbid, steaming and clearing within.

Category: Wind — Ascending — Generating

Large nose, small tail, female genitalia, small testicles, slightly drowsy appearance; it is similar in form to a yellow dog but smaller.

Meat:

Dispelling Wind

Five Organs: Nature slightly cold; taste bitter; toxic. Mainly treats gu toxin (parasitic poison) and childhood fright-epilepsy. Burning the liver to ash treats wind conditions.

Gallbladder: Used to revive people. In cases of sudden collapse, administer raw; grind and pour in, wait for revival.

Intestines and Stomach: Nature benefits children. Treats fright-epilepsy and slight cold. Mainly treats malaria; also treats scabies and [related conditions].

Head and Tail: Burning is harmful. The male [otter], in the correct month, is used as a courier [remedy].

Lips: Cutting out [and using]; burning away foul odors. Treats epidemic illness, upward-rushing qi. The male [otter], taste sweet; those who say it treats chronic illness, stops worms, preserves for long periods; mainly treats [the above conditions].

Excrement: Burning it is good. In cases of epidemic foul qi from enclosed spaces, the male [otter] in the correct month is also used. Has [effect on] fatigue-illness, stops worms, main treatment; use fish as ritual offering.

Otter Liver: [For] epidemic contagion spreading from person to person; nature [cold]; treats consumption and wasting disease conditions through sequential transmission. Used with appropriate medicines to treat extreme fatigue.

Heavenly Gu Toxin: Treats strange scabies; among the five domestic animals — dogs and meat — all have [slightly cold nature]; only [the otter's] nature is warm; the medicine should be stopped if corpse-fatigue symptoms occur; the medicine treats extreme fatigue.

Second Month: Mainly benefits birthing [animals]; among the six domestic animals, the medicine is sometimes used; also has the property of reducing [conditions]; it must match this form to be effective; verified by [the source text].

Flesh — Gallbladder — Kidney — Bone — Marrow — Four Feet (Limbs) — Skin

[Flesh:] It is good for deficiency conditions. Its nature is neutral and non-toxic. It mainly treats bone-steaming fever; when decocted and consumed, it benefits the blood and vessels. It is suitable for women and children to eat regularly.

[Gallbladder:] Its nature is cold. It mainly treats water retention and bloating in the lower abdomen. When the hot swelling subsides, the qi and fluids are regulated. It benefits men and is good for the eyes. When administered as a decoction, it treats suppurating sores, swellings, and masses on the face.

[Kidney:] It mainly treats the eyes and improves vision. Combined with wine, taken with a slight increase in dose, it has been shown to be effective. Ancient formulas mention using it with flying rope hemp and ox bile. Tests show results, though not always verified. It treats carbuncles, hard nodes, and facial ulcers.

[Bone:] It mainly promotes marrow growth, which is difficult. The white layer is applied as a paste. It is hard to use medicinally.

[Marrow:] It reduces and treats swellings. It is applied as a paste. Taken with bone broth, it is beneficial.

[Four Feet:] The main fish bones are cooked and the broth drunk. The juice is boiled and applied.

[Skin:] It is used so that the skin of people, taken from the eel, day by day adorns and smooths the body. It repels dust and wind, so that not even road dust clings to it; it is said to be effective for the complexion.

Cat Meat
It is also called by other names. Its nature is balanced, taste sweet and pungent; it is said to be non-toxic. It is mainly used for long-standing water swelling and toxic conditions. Taken in sufficient quantity, it is extremely nourishing. Used to treat long-standing ringworm. Eaten regularly, it reduces abdominal bloating. Also known locally as "earth pig" or wild cat.

Fat and Grease (of Cat)
Eating it is a fine tonic. It nourishes muscles and flesh, making the body fat and full. The white meat with yellow broth made into a soup and eaten regularly achieves this.

Bladder
When dried and emptied, it is used mainly to draw in qi, check demonic influences, and treat childhood nutritional disorders (gan) and related conditions.

Badger Meat
Its fur is used to make fur garments. Sweet in taste; it primarily governs the viscera, invigorates the spirit, and treats many types of conditions including vacuity swellings (yong) in women. Its shape and coloring resemble a small fox. Used popularly to treat emaciation in children and to relieve swelling. Commonly called "mountain dog." Its flavor is mild.

Raccoon Dog (Hǒ) Meat
Its fur is also used similarly. Sweet in taste; it primarily governs the viscera, invigorates the spirit, and treats many types of conditions including vacuity swellings in women. Its shape and coloring resemble a small fox.

Fur Seal Kidney (Wǎnà Qí)
Its nature is greatly warming, taste salty; said to be non-toxic. It mainly treats the five strains and seven injuries, decline of kidney essence and weakness, depletion of kidney qi, and excessive sexual indulgence. It assists yang qi, relieves lumbar and kidney soreness, itching, weakness of the knees and bladder, and cold in the fox-cold pattern. Also known in Silla (ancient Korea) as "sea dog outer kidney." It is taken together with the testes to assist [the yang].
